subs.text: Every Halloween for seven years,
at exactly 11:47 at night,
someone knocked on Walter Greene's door.
It was always the same trick-or-treater.
A small figure in a pumpkin mask, and a brown coat far too big for it.
It never said trick or treat. It never said thank you.
It just held out an old white pillowcase, and waited.
And every year, Walter noticed the same impossible thing.
The child never grew. Not an inch. Not in seven years.
This is the story of an old man,
a quiet little town in Vermont,
and a trick-or-treater who came back every Halloween.
And it's the story of what that old man found,
when he finally decided to follow it home.
This is the story of the last trick-or-treater of Maple Falls, Vermont.
And it begins, of all things, with a scarecrow.
Walter Greene lived in the same white
farmhouse on Orchard Lane for twenty-six years.
At the edge of town, where the houses ended and the fields began.
He and his wife, Margaret, never had children of their own.
So every Halloween, they made the whole town's children their own.
Margaret baked caramel apples for three days straight.
Walter carved pumpkins until his hands ached.
The porch looked like a pumpkin patch.
And every year, Walter wore the same costume. A scarecrow.
Margaret had sewn it for him in 1962,
their first Halloween in the house, straw hat and all.
Kids from all over Maple Falls walked the long road to Orchard Lane,
just to get a caramel apple from the scarecrow and his wife.
In the spring of 1988, Margaret passed away in her sleep.
She was sixty-six. The whole town came to say goodbye.
That October, Walter didn't carve a single pumpkin.
The porch stayed dark.
The scarecrow costume stayed folded in the cedar chest upstairs.
But on the morning of Halloween,
a little girl from down the road left a drawing in his mailbox.
A scarecrow, holding a caramel apple.
Walter looked at that drawing for a long time.
Then he went upstairs, opened the cedar chest, and took out the straw hat.
He couldn't make caramel apples the way Margaret did.
So he drove to the store and bought the biggest chocolate bars they had.
That night, the scarecrow of Orchard Lane opened his door again.
And the children came, just like always.
It was a good night. The best he'd had since spring.
Witches, cowboys,
and a tiny astronaut who made him laugh until he had to sit down.
By eleven, the last of the kids had gone home.
Walter sat on the porch swing in his scarecrow costume,
with half a bowl of candy left.
He talked to Margaret for a while. Out loud.
He told her about the astronaut.
He told her he missed her. The field was silent.
At eleven forty, he blew out the candles and went inside.
He hung the straw hat on the hook by the door, and put the kettle on.
At exactly 11:47, there was a knock. Three soft knocks.
Low on the door, too low for a grown-up.
Walter looked at the clock.
On the porch stood a child in a papier-mache pumpkin mask,
holding out an old white pillowcase.
The mask was homemade.
Faded orange paint, a crooked painted smile, two dark holes for eyes.
The kind of mask nobody had made in decades.
The child wore a man's brown wool coat,
so big the sleeves were rolled up four times,
and the hem dragged on the porch boards.
Walter smiled and asked where the child's folks were.
It was awfully late. The child didn't answer.
It just held the pillowcase a little higher.
So Walter dropped in a chocolate bar.
For a second, a breath of cold air came out of the pillowcase.
Like air from a cellar.
The child turned and walked down the steps.
Not toward the road, where the houses were.
Toward the empty field behind the house.
Walter grabbed his flashlight and called after it.
But by the time he reached the steps, the field was empty.
Just grass and moonlight.
He told himself it was a neighbor's kid playing a prank.
And he kept telling himself that for almost a year.
Halloween, 1989. Walter wore his scarecrow costume again.
The kids came again.
And at exactly 11:47, there were three soft knocks.
Same pumpkin mask.
Same brown coat, with the sleeves rolled up four times.
Same white pillowcase. Walter's heart started pounding.
This time he noticed something else. The coat was damp.
Not from rain, it hadn't rained in weeks.
It smelled like cold, wet stone.
He put a chocolate bar in the pillowcase
and watched the child walk toward the field.
This time, he followed it to the fence.
It walked straight into the tall grass.
The grass didn't move. The dry leaves didn't crunch.
And halfway across the field, it was just gone.
It walked into the field without bending a single blade of grass.
And then, it simply wasn't there anymore.
Walter didn't sleep that night.
He sat at the kitchen table with a notebook,
and wrote down everything he could remember.
The time. The coat. The smell.
The way the smile on the mask was painted a little crooked on the left.
He dated the page. October 31st, 1989.
Halloween, 1990.
Walter waited by the door with his notebook.
At 11:47, three soft knocks.
He wrote down the time before he opened the door.
The year before,
he had marked the child's height on the porch post with a pencil.
He checked it again. Exactly the same.
Halloween, 1991. The same. Halloween, 1992. The same.
The kids who came earlier in the evening were growing up.
They got taller every year.
But the child in the pumpkin mask stayed exactly the same height.
Four feet and two inches. Year after year after year.
In 1992, Walter finally asked. What's your name, son?
The child raised one small hand in the wool sleeve, and pointed at the field.
It didn't say a word. It only pointed at the field.
And Walter understood that it wanted him to follow.
But Walter was seventy-two, the field was dark, and something in him was afraid.
So he closed the door. And he hated himself for it.
That winter, he started asking questions. Carefully.
He didn't want the town to think the old scarecrow had lost his mind.
He asked his neighbors if a family with a little boy lived nearby.
Nobody knew of one. Not on Orchard Lane.
Not for a very long time.
So he drove to the Maple Falls public library and asked
the librarian to help him look through the old newspapers on microfilm.
He didn't know what he was looking for.
So he started with Halloween.
Every November first, of every year, going back as far as they had.
It took him three weeks. Then,
in the paper from November 2nd, 1951,
he found a headline that made his hands go cold.
Local boy missing on Halloween night.
Nine-year-old Billy Harlan.
Last seen walking alone on Orchard Lane, at about a quarter to midnight.
There was a photograph. A small,
freckled boy grinning at the camera,
holding up a homemade papier-mache pumpkin mask.
The same mask.
The article said Billy had worn his late father's brown wool coat that night,
because it was cold. Sleeves rolled up four times.
Walter sat in the dark library for a long time.
The boy had been gone for forty-one years.
And he was still out trick-or-treating.
The article mentioned Billy's older sister, Dorothy.
It took Walter two months, but he found her.
A retired schoolteacher living in Burlington.
He almost didn't go. What could he possibly say?
Your little brother knocks on my door every Halloween?
She'd call the police on him.
But in March of 1994,
he drove up to Burlington with a box of chocolates,
and the old newspaper clipping folded in his coat pocket.
Dorothy Harlan was small and sharp-eyed.
She looked at the clipping, then at Walter, and said quietly: You've seen him.
Haven't you?
Walter told her everything. The knocks. The mask.
The pillowcase. The field.
She listened without interrupting, holding his hand the whole time.
Then she told him what happened in 1951.
Billy had begged to go out alone that year. Just once.
He was nine. He was big enough, he said.
He wanted to go to one last house.
The old Kessler farmhouse, out past the end of Orchard Lane.
The Kesslers always gave out popcorn balls.
The Kessler house burned down in 1960, two years before Walter moved in.
Today it was just an empty field.
The field behind his house.
Dorothy said the whole town had searched for a month.
The woods, the river, every barn and cellar in Maple Falls.
They never found anything.
Their mother never moved away.
Every Halloween until the day she died,
she left the porch light on all night,
in case Billy found his way home.
Before he left, she squeezed his hand. Please, she said.
If he comes again, go with him.
He's been waiting a long time for someone to follow.
Dorothy Harlan had waited forty-three years for an answer.
She asked Walter for only one thing: to follow him.
Halloween, 1994. Walter was seventy-four.
He put on the scarecrow costume one more time,
and handed out candy to the children, just like always.
At eleven thirty, he put on his warm boots,
put new batteries in his flashlight,
and sat by the door with his coat on.
The field behind the house was silver with frost.
The moon was full.
A thin fog was lying low over the grass, like water.
At 11:47, three soft knocks. Walter opened the door.
The small figure in the pumpkin mask was standing there,
holding out its pillowcase.
Walter dropped in a chocolate bar. Then he knelt down,
so the mask was level with his eyes,
and said quietly: Okay, Billy. Show me.
For the first time in seven years, the child didn't vanish.
It walked slowly into the fog. And Walter followed.
They crossed the field together.
The old man in the scarecrow hat,
and the small figure in the pumpkin mask,
side by side in the fog.
The grass around Walter crunched with frost.
Around the child, there was no sound at all.
Walter's breath came out in white clouds.
The child's didn't.
Halfway across, the fog grew thicker.
Walter could barely see his own hands.
But the pumpkin mask seemed to glow faintly, just ahead of him.
Then the child stopped.
In the middle of the field was something Walter had walked past a hundred times,
and never really seen.
An old stone well. Covered with rotting gray boards.
Half hidden by weeds and brambles.
It must have belonged to the Kessler farm.
The child pointed down at the boards.
Then, right before Walter's eyes, it faded into the fog.
Walter stood alone in the field.
On the gray boards of the well lay the old white pillowcase.
And beside it, the pumpkin mask.
He picked up the mask with trembling hands.
The papier-mache was soft and damp.
The inside smelled like cold, wet stone.
Just like the coat.
He didn't try to open the well.
He sat down on the frosty grass beside it,
holding the mask in his lap, and waited for morning.
At sunrise, he walked back to the house,
still wearing the straw hat,
and called the county sheriff.
Sheriff Tom Brady had known Walter for thirty years.
He didn't laugh.
He looked at the mask for a long time, and then he made some calls.
By noon, there were trucks in the field.
Men with ropes and lights pulled the gray boards off the old Kessler well,
for the first time in decades.
The well had been dry for decades. At the bottom,
under forty-three autumns of leaves,
they found what the whole town had searched for in 1951.
Billy had fallen into the old well in the dark that night,
on his way to one last house.
After forty-three years, he could finally come home.
Billy Harlan was laid to rest in November of 1994,
next to his mother and father,
in the old Maple Falls cemetery on the hill.
Dorothy drove down from Burlington.
Walter walked beside her up the hill, through the red and yellow leaves.
She asked Walter to put one thing in with her brother.
Not flowers. The pumpkin mask. He'd want it, she said.
It was his favorite.
After the service, she held Walter's hand and cried.
Thank you, she said.
You're the only one who ever followed him.
Walter left one more thing on the grave. A chocolate bar.
The biggest one they sold.
Halloween, 1995.
Walter put on his scarecrow costume and handed
out candy to every child in Maple Falls.
Then he sat by the door, and waited.
Eleven forty-five. Eleven forty-six. Eleven forty-seven.
The field was quiet. Nobody knocked.
Walter sat there until one in the morning.
He should have felt relieved. And he was.
But he also felt something he didn't expect.
He missed him. He missed his little visitor.
Walter handed out candy for three more Halloweens.
Every year, at 11:47, he looked at the door.
And every year, nobody knocked.
In the spring of 1998,
Walter Greene passed away peacefully in his armchair,
with the window open to the field. He was seventy-eight.
Half the town came to say goodbye.
Grown men and women who had once gotten
caramel apples from the scarecrow on Orchard Lane.
Somebody left his old straw hat on the steps of the church.
Nobody knew who. Nobody remembered bringing it.
But nobody moved it, either.
That summer,
the white farmhouse on Orchard Lane was sold to a young family from Boston.
The Morales family.
Two parents and an eight-year-old girl named Sofia.
They loved the house. The big porch. The swing.
The field out back, where Sofia played all summer long.
The neighbors told them about Walter. The scarecrow.
The caramel apples.
They said Orchard Lane had always been the best street for Halloween.
So on Halloween, 1998,
the Morales family carved twelve pumpkins,
and turned on every light on the porch.
Sofia dressed up as a witch.
The kids came from all over town.
It was a wonderful night.
By eleven, Sofia had fallen asleep on the couch in her witch hat.
Her mother, Elena, was cleaning up the kitchen when she heard it.
Three soft knocks at the front door.
She looked at the clock. It was 11:47.
On the porch stood two trick-or-treaters.
A small one in a pumpkin mask. And a tall scarecrow.
The tall one wore a battered straw hat and a patched denim jacket,
with straw sticking out of the sleeves.
Its face was hidden under the brim.
The small one held out an old white pillowcase.
The tall one held out its hand.
It was an old man's hand, wrinkled and gentle.
Elena didn't scream.
She said later she couldn't explain it, but she wasn't afraid.
She put a chocolate bar in each of their hands.
The scarecrow tipped its straw hat to her.
Then the two of them turned and walked down the porch steps,
side by side, toward the field.
They walked into the field together, the old man and the boy.
And halfway across, they were gone.
In the morning, Elena went out to the field.
The frost was untouched. No footprints.
Just two chocolate wrappers, folded neatly on the fence post.
She told the neighbors.
The old woman next door started to cry, then laughed.
Walter always said he'd go trick-or-treating someday, she said.
The Morales family still lives in the white house on Orchard Lane.
And every Halloween, they keep the porch light on until midnight.
Sofia is grown now.
But she still comes home every October thirty-first,
and sits on the porch swing with a bowl of the biggest chocolate bars in town.
At 11:47, there are always three soft knocks.
Two trick-or-treaters. A small one in a pumpkin mask.
A tall one in a straw hat.
They never say trick or treat. They never say thank you.
But the scarecrow always tips his hat.
And the boy always waves goodbye.
People in Maple Falls don't talk about it much.
But on Halloween,
nobody on Orchard Lane turns their porch light off before midnight.
Because they know that somewhere out there,
two old friends are still walking from house to house.
Just like they always wanted to.
So this Halloween, if you're handing out candy late,
and you hear three soft knocks close to midnight,
don't be afraid.
Just leave the porch light on a little longer.
Somebody's still out there, trick-or-treating.
And if the smaller one holds out an old white pillowcase,
give it something sweet.
He waited a very long time for that one last house.
Happy Halloween. Leave your porch light on until midnight.
And if you hear three soft knocks at 11:47, you'll know who it is.
